nameStory: The "bleeding heart" name comes from the flower's distinctive shape that looks just like a pink heart with a droplet hanging from its tip, as if the heart is bleeding. The "fringed" part refers to the delicately cut, lacy edges of its fernlike leaves that look like they've been trimmed with fine scissors.
description: Fringed bleeding heart is a charming woodland wildflower that produces clusters of pink, heart-shaped flowers dangling from arching stems. This native perennial grows in low mounds about 12-18 inches tall and wide, with delicate, blue-green leaves that are so finely divided they look almost like fern fronds. Unlike the common garden bleeding heart, this wild cousin blooms repeatedly throughout the growing season and thrives in our New England woodlands.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pink heart-shaped flowers with a white or pale pink droplet hanging from the bottom, dangling in loose clusters above the foliage. Each flower is about half an inch long and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, fernlike leaves with a soft, blue-green color that feel delicate and slightly waxy. The leaf segments are so narrow and intricate they create an almost lacy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, mounded clumps that spread slowly by underground rhizomes. Plants typically stay under 2 feet tall but can form colonies over time.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, narrow capsules that split open to release tiny black seeds. The capsules are easy to miss among the delicate foliage.

habitat: Look for fringed bleeding heart in rich, moist deciduous woodlands, especially on rocky slopes and in mountain coves throughout New England's higher elevations. It thrives in the dappled shade under hardwood trees like maples and oaks, often growing alongside wild ginger, trilliums, and ferns in areas with well-draining but consistently moist soil.

seasonality.spring: First flowers appear in late April to May as the delicate foliage emerges. The blue-green leaves unfurl like tiny fern fiddleheads.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming sporadically through summer, with the most abundant flower display typically in early summer. Foliage remains fresh and attractive.
seasonality.fall: May produce a second flush of blooms in early fall. Leaves gradually yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. Look for small reddish buds just at soil level in late winter.

funFact: Unlike most wildflowers that bloom once per season, fringed bleeding heart can produce flowers from spring through fall, making it one of the longest-blooming native wildflowers in New England forests!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the common garden bleeding heart, but wild fringed bleeding heart has much more finely divided, blue-green leaves (versus the garden variety's broader, yellow-green leaflets) and continues blooming all season instead of just spring. Remember: wild and finely divided versus garden and broadly divided.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native treasure with the Asian bleeding heart commonly sold in garden centers. Our native fringed bleeding heart is much better adapted to New England conditions and supports local wildlife, while the garden variety typically goes dormant by midsummer.
compareHints: Fringed bleeding heart differs from its cousins Dutchman's breeches and squirrel corn by blooming throughout the growing season rather than just early spring, and by its pink heart-shaped flowers instead of white pantaloon or kernel-shaped blooms. While Dutchman's breeches and squirrel corn go completely dormant by early summer, fringed bleeding heart keeps its attractive foliage all season long.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to squirrel corn, Dutchman's breeches has more distinctly "pantaloon-shaped" flowers with pointed spurs versus squirrel corn's heart-shaped blooms with rounded spurs.

Squirrel corn differs from Dutchman's breeches primarily in flower shape - squirrel corn has heart-shaped flowers with rounded spurs, while Dutchman's breeches has pantaloon-shaped flowers with pointed spurs.
Pacific Bleeding Heart differs from its New England relatives by blooming later and longer than the early spring ephemerals Dutchman's Breeches and Squirrel Corn, which go dormant by early summer.
